sections.h2: What eviction notice does a New Hampshire landlord have to give?
sections.html:
A New Hampshire landlord has to give the tenant a written eviction notice before going to court, and for a residential rental the notice must be 30 days, or 7 days when the reason is nonpayment, substantial damage or behavior that harms the health or safety of others. The rule sits in RSA 540:3.

The notice is only the first step. A tenant does not have to leave on the date written in it, and a landlord who wants the house back must still bring a court case after the notice runs out. If you own a rented house and want to sell it, the notice you serve decides how soon the court process can even begin.

This page covers the notice itself. The court steps that follow are on our separate New Hampshire eviction process page.

sections.h2: Which notice period applies to which reason?
sections.html:
The period depends on the reason written in the notice, and the reasons are listed in RSA 540:2. The table below pulls the main ones together.

Reason for the noticeNotice periodStatute
Nonpayment of rent after demand7 daysRSA 540:2, II(a) and 540:3, II
Substantial damage to the premises7 daysRSA 540:2, II(b) and 540:3, II
Behavior that harms the health or safety of others7 daysRSA 540:2, II(d) and 540:3, II
Failure to follow a material lease term30 daysRSA 540:2, II(c) and 540:3, II
Other good cause30 daysRSA 540:2, II(e) and 540:3, II
End of a lease of 12 months or longerWritten notice at least 60 days before the term endsRSA 540:2, II(i)

Ordinary rent that is simply late does not shortcut the process. The nonpayment ground applies to rent that is due and overdue, and the landlord has to make a demand for it. A demand for rent can be served at any time after the rent is due, and before or at the same time as the eviction notice (RSA 540:5).

sections.h2: Does the landlord need a reason at all?
sections.html:
It depends on the kind of property. RSA 540:2 splits rentals into nonrestricted and restricted property, and only restricted property requires a listed reason.

Under RSA 540:1-a, restricted property means real property rented for residential purposes, except a few categories. The excluded, nonrestricted categories are:

  • Property rented for nonresidential purposes.
  • A single-family house, if the owner does not own more than three single-family houses at one time.
  • A rental unit in an owner-occupied building with four or fewer dwelling units.
  • A single-family house a bank or other mortgagee acquired through foreclosure.

For nonrestricted property, the owner may end the tenancy by written notice without giving a reason (RSA 540:2, I). Whether your house falls in the single-family exclusion depends on how many single-family houses you own, so count them before you decide which notice to prepare. The 603 Legal Aid guide, though, lists a single-family home rented with the landlord living elsewhere among the tenancies that still need a judge before the tenant must leave, so the court step applies even where the reason does not.

sections.h2: What does the notice have to say?
sections.html:
The notice must state the reason for the eviction with specificity, and if the reason is nonpayment it must tell the tenant about any right to avoid eviction by paying the arrears and liquidated damages (RSA 540:3, III and IV). A vague line such as "violation of lease" invites a defense. A line naming the lease term, the date and what happened gives the court something to read.

Delivery has fewer rules than most landlords expect. Under RSA 540:5, any person may serve a residential notice, and it can be handed to the tenant or left at the tenant's last and usual place of abode. Proof of service is a true, attested copy of the notice plus an affidavit of service, which does not need to be sworn.

  • The district court provides demand-for-rent and eviction-notice forms at clerks' offices and on the Judicial Branch website.
  • Landlords do not have to use the court forms, but a valid notice needs the same information the forms ask for.
  • The 603 Legal Aid guide adds that a spoken order to leave does not count. The notice has to be written.

sections.h2: How does a lease-ending notice work when the lease runs 12 months or more?
sections.html:
A landlord can end a lease of 12 months or longer at expiration only by giving written notice at least 60 days before the term ends and by filing the court case within 6 months after expiration (RSA 540:2, II(i)). Shorter leases renewed to a total of 12 months or more are treated the same way.

This ground is useful for an owner who wants to sell with a vacant house. The dates are strict. Miss the 60 days and the notice is short. Wait past six months and the case window closes. Retaliation and discrimination defenses stay available to the tenant even on a clean lease-end notice.

The statute also says a termination under this ground cannot count as an eviction on a rental application or tenant screening report, and the court must note in its record that the end of the tenancy was not the tenant's fault.

sections.h2: What counts as other good cause, and can a rent increase be one?
sections.html:
"Other good cause" is a catch-all ground, and the statute gives it real content. Under RSA 540:2, V, it includes, but is not limited to, a legitimate business or economic reason, and it does not have to involve anything the tenant did.

Two limits apply. If the cause is the tenant's conduct, the landlord must first have given written notice that more conduct of that kind would be grounds for eviction (RSA 540:2, III). And a tenant's refusal to accept a rent increase can be good cause only if the landlord gave written notice of the amount and the effective date at least 30 days beforehand (RSA 540:2, IV).

Selling the house can be a business reason in principle, but the statute does not name a sale, so a landlord relying on it should write the reason plainly and expect a judge to test it. A New Hampshire attorney can confirm the wording before you serve.

sections.h2: What can stop or defeat an eviction notice?
sections.html:
Several statutory protections can end an eviction case even when the notice was served correctly.

  • Cure of nonpayment: a tenant can stop a nonpayment case by paying all rent due, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and the landlord's filing and service fees before the hearing. The cure works up to 3 times in a 12-month period (RSA 540:9).
  • Retaliation: it is a defense if the action followed the tenant reporting a violation, using RSA 540-A or meeting with other tenants, except where the tenant owes a week's rent or more (RSA 540:13-a).
  • Habitability: a tenant can defend a nonpayment case where substantial code violations materially affect habitability, written notice was given and the landlord did not fix the problem within 14 days. The court may pause the case for up to a month for repairs (RSA 540:13-d).
  • Utility payments: a tenancy cannot be ended for nonpayment if the tenant paid the landlord's utility bill to prevent a shutoff, the arrears do not exceed that payment and the tenant has proof (RSA 540:2, VI).
  • Domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking: a tenant who is a victim and provides qualifying verification cannot be evicted solely for that reason (RSA 540:2, VII).

sections.h2: How does a pending notice affect selling the rented house?
sections.html:
A pending notice does not stop you from selling, but you cannot hand a buyer a vacant house until the court process finishes or the tenant leaves. Plan the sale around that timing and around what you may and may not do in the meantime.

RSA 540-A:3 bars a landlord from willfully cutting off utilities, locking a tenant out or seizing the premises or the tenant's property without proper judicial process. It also limits entry without consent, which matters if you want to show the house. The 603 Legal Aid guide says the landlord may not change locks until a sheriff has served and carried out the writ of possession. When a tenant leaves, the landlord must take reasonable care of belongings for 7 days (RSA 540-A:3, VII).

A cash sale gives a seller two practical paths. One is to sell with the tenant in place, as is, to a buyer who wants a rental. The other is to finish the notice and court steps first, then sell vacant. We buy New Hampshire houses in either condition, and a call can help you compare the timelines before you serve anything. We do not promise a price or a closing date on a page, and any offer is made after we see the house.

faqs.q: How many days of notice does a landlord have to give in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: For residential tenancies, 30 days is enough in all cases, and 7 days is enough when the reason is nonpayment of rent, substantial damage or behavior that harms the health or safety of others (RSA 540:3, II).

faqs.q: Does a New Hampshire eviction notice have to be on a court form?
faqs.a: No. Landlords are not required to use the court forms, but a valid notice must contain the same information the forms request, including the reason stated with specificity.

faqs.q: Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent?
faqs.a: Yes, in a nonpayment case. The tenant can pay all rent due, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and the landlord's filing and service fees before the hearing. This cure is limited to 3 times in 12 months (RSA 540:9).

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict at the end of a lease just to sell the house?
faqs.a: Only under the lease-expiration ground, which applies to leases of 12 months or longer. The landlord must give written notice at least 60 days before the term ends and file the court case within 6 months after expiration. The tenant can still raise retaliation or discrimination defenses.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks after the eviction notice runs out?
faqs.a: No. The notice expiring does not end the tenancy by itself. According to 603 Legal Aid, locks may be changed only after a sheriff has served and carried out a writ of possession, and RSA 540-A:3 bars lockouts without judicial process.
